options.content: One that must by law be reported
Any disease a farmer can treat on the farm
A disease that affects only poultry
A disease caused only by poor feeding

explanation: Notifiable (scheduled) diseases are listed in animal health law and must be reported when suspected.

stem: Which animals are affected by foot-and-mouth disease?

options.content: Cloven-hoofed animals such as cattle and pigs
Poultry such as chickens and turkeys
Donkeys and horses only
options.rationale: Horses and donkeys are not cloven-hoofed.

options.content: Rabbits only

explanation: FMD affects cloven-hoofed animals: cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and wild species such as buffalo.

stem: Trypanosomiasis in cattle is spread by:

options.content: the blue tick
options.rationale: The blue tick spreads redwater and gallsickness.

options.content: contaminated drinking water
options.rationale: Trypanosomes are carried in blood by flies.

options.content: the mosquito
options.rationale: Mosquitoes are not the vector of nagana.

options.content: the tsetse fly

explanation: Tsetse flies carry trypanosomes from animal to animal when they feed on blood.

stem: A cow is found dead with dark, unclotted blood oozing from her nose and anus. What should the farmer do?

options.content: Skin it at once so that the hide can still be sold for cash
options.rationale: Opening releases spores and risks human infection.

options.content: Keep everyone away and report it, without opening it
Cut it open to find the cause of death
options.rationale: Never open a suspected anthrax carcass.

options.content: Leave it in the paddock for the dogs to clear

explanation: These signs suggest anthrax. Opening the carcass lets the bacteria form spores that contaminate soil for years and can infect people.
hints: Which notifiable disease causes sudden death with unclotted blood?

stem: Antibodies a calf receives in colostrum give it which type of immunity?

options.content: Natural active immunity
options.rationale: Active immunity is made by the calf itself.

options.content: Natural passive immunity
options.rationale: Correct: ready-made antibodies from the mother.

options.content: Artificial active immunity
Artificial passive immunity

explanation: Colostral antibodies are made by the mother and received naturally: natural passive immunity.

stem: Why must a newborn calf suck colostrum within the first few hours of birth?

options.content: Colostrum turns into poison after one day
options.rationale: It does not; it changes to normal milk.

options.content: The calf can digest no other kind of feed for a whole month
options.rationale: Calves drink normal milk after colostrum.

options.content: Its gut can absorb whole antibodies only briefly
options.rationale: Correct: absorption falls quickly in the first day.

options.content: Colostrum vaccinates the mother as well
options.rationale: Sucking does not vaccinate the cow.

explanation: The newborn's gut absorbs antibodies whole for only a short time, so early feeding gives the most protection.
hints: What happens to the calf's gut lining soon after birth?

stem: Why do veterinary services stop cattle movements in a district where foot-and-mouth disease is found?

options.content: To make the cattle grow faster
options.rationale: Movement control is not for growth.

options.content: Because the disease affects only moving cattle
options.rationale: All exposed cloven-hoofed animals are at risk.

options.content: To stop infected animals spreading the virus
options.rationale: Correct: the virus spreads with animals and vehicles.

options.content: To prevent tsetse flies following the cattle

explanation: FMD spreads very readily with live animals, products, people and vehicles; stopping movement contains the outbreak.
hints: How does FMD spread between farms?

stem: A donkey that has never been vaccinated against tetanus gets a deep, dirty wound. The vet injects tetanus antitoxin (ready-made antibodies) at once and starts a course of vaccine. Why is the antitoxin given?

options.content: They give protection for the rest of the donkey's life
They make the vaccine unnecessary
options.rationale: The vaccine gives lasting active immunity.

options.content: They make the wound heal faster
options.rationale: They neutralise the toxin; they do not heal tissue.

options.content: They protect at once while the vaccine takes effect

explanation: Active immunity from vaccine takes days to develop; injected antibodies (artificial passive immunity) protect immediately but briefly.
hints: Compare how quickly active and passive immunity work.

stem: Vaccination is used to cure animals that are already sick with Newcastle disease.
explanation: False. Vaccines prevent disease in healthy birds; there is no cure for Newcastle disease.

stem: Match each notifiable disease with its cause.
explanation: Learn the type of organism for each named disease.

payload.template: Immunity that an animal makes itself after vaccination is called artificial {{blank:a}} immunity; antibodies received in colostrum give natural {{blank:b}} immunity.

explanation: Vaccination: artificial active. Colostrum: natural passive.

stem: Hens in a flock gasp, twist their necks, pass greenish diarrhoea and many die; egg laying falls sharply. Name the notifiable viral disease these signs suggest.
hints: It is prevented by vaccinating chicks.

stem: A farmer must vaccinate 2,300 chickens. Assume the vaccine comes in vials of 1,000 doses. How many vials must be bought? (Round UP to whole vials.)
explanation: 2,300 ÷ 1,000 = 2.3, so 3 vials; 2 vials would leave 300 birds unprotected.
workedSolution: 1. 2,300 ÷ 1,000 = 2.3, so 3 vials; 2 vials would leave 300 birds unprotected.

stem: In a dip-tank area, 342 of 380 cattle are vaccinated against anthrax. Calculate the percentage vaccinated.
A vaccine for cattle is given at 2 mL per animal (assume). A farmer has 145 cattle and the vaccine is sold in 100 mL bottles. How many bottles must he buy?
workedSolution:
1. Volume needed = 2 mL × 145 = 290 mL.
2. Bottles = 290 ÷ 100 = 2.9.
3. Round up: 3 bottles (2 bottles would leave 45 cattle without vaccine).
hints: Total volume = dose × number of cattle.

stem: Explain **two** reasons why some livestock diseases are made notifiable by law.

points.description: They spread rapidly over large areas / between farms.
So control needs government powers such as quarantine and movement control.
Some can infect people (e.g. anthrax, rabies) / cause heavy losses.
Outbreaks close export markets for meat and animals, harming the whole country's farmers.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Diseases such as foot-and-mouth spread very quickly between farms, so only the government can stop them with quarantine and movement control. Others, like anthrax, can kill people, and outbreaks close export markets for meat, harming every farmer in the country.

hints: Think of people, spread and trade.

stem: Describe **four** good practices when vaccinating a flock of chickens through their drinking water.

points.description: Keep the vaccine cool and out of sunlight; check the expiry date.
Use clean water with no disinfectant or chlorine, in clean drinkers.
Withhold water for a short time first so the birds drink the vaccine quickly; give enough drinkers for all birds.
Vaccinate only healthy birds at the right age, give boosters as directed, and record the date and batch number.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Keep the vaccine cool and in date, mix it in clean water without disinfectant, withhold water briefly so all birds drink it quickly from enough clean drinkers, and vaccinate healthy birds at the right age, recording the date and batch.

explanation: Cold chain, clean water, uptake, records.

stem: Several cattle at a farm near Chipinge are drooling, limping and have blisters on their tongues and between their hooves. The dairy cows' milk yield has fallen sharply. Buffalo from a nearby conservancy sometimes break through the farm fence.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the disease these signs suggest.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What type of organism causes this disease?

options.content: A bacterium
A protozoan
A roundworm
A virus

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest how the disease probably reached the farm, and one way to prevent this.

points.description: Buffalo can carry the virus and passed it to the cattle by contact / sharing grazing and water.
Repair and strengthen (game-proof) the fence / keep cattle away from buffalo areas.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State the farmer's legal duty and **one** action he must take while waiting for the veterinary officer.

points.description: Report the suspected disease to the veterinary services at once (it is notifiable).
Keep the cattle confined / do not move or sell animals, milk or products / stop visitors and vehicles.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why an outbreak on one farm can affect every cattle farmer in the country.

points.description: The virus spreads rapidly to neighbouring farms by animals, people, vehicles and products.
Movement controls and quarantine stop sales and auctions over a wide area.
Importing countries ban the country's beef, so export markets are lost / prices fall.

explanation: Identify a notifiable disease and explain the farmer's duty and the wider effects.
hints: Which notifiable disease causes blisters on the mouth and feet?

stem: Farai keeps 640 indigenous chickens near Masvingo. The veterinary officer advises vaccinating against Newcastle disease. Assume the vaccine comes in vials of 200 doses, one dose per bird. Last year a calf on the same farm died of scours after its mother died at birth.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many vials must Farai buy?

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How many doses will be left over?

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain what type of immunity the vaccine gives the chickens.

points.description: The birds' own bodies make antibodies (and memory) in response to the weakened virus, giving long-lasting protection.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why the orphaned calf died of scours, and what Farai should do for orphaned calves in future.

points.description: It received no colostrum, so it had no antibodies (no passive immunity) against scours pathogens.
Feed colostrum from another cow (or stored frozen colostrum) within the first few hours of birth.

explanation: Plan a vaccination and explain active and passive immunity.
hints: What does a newborn calf miss if its mother dies?
